idiom_name: trait Renderer + Box<dyn Renderer> in the abstraction
implementation_notes: The implementor is a trait holding the primitive operations, and the abstraction is a struct that owns the implementor either as a trait object (Box<dyn Renderer>, a fat pointer carrying data plus a vtable, dynamic dispatch) or through a generic type parameter (R: Renderer, monomorphised static dispatch with no lookup at all). The Rust Book's trait-object chapter states the trade-off directly: trait objects allow a heterogeneous collection or a runtime-chosen type at the cost of a vtable lookup and blocked inlining, while generics are preferable whenever a single concrete type suffices. The trait replaces the abstract Implementor base; when the implementor set is closed and you own it, an enum plus match is the most idiomatic form - no allocation, no vtable, exhaustiveness checked - so keep the dyn form where implementations are chosen at runtime or come from outside the crate.
pitfalls: dyn Trait values are unsized and must live behind a pointer; the auto-trait and lifetime components (+ Send + Sync + 'static) are part of the type, so decide them at the abstraction boundary or every holder changes.

A trait that is not dyn-compatible (a method returning Self, or a generic method) cannot be used as Box<dyn Trait> at all; the fixes are where Self: Sized on that method so it leaves the vtable, or an object-safe clone_box replacement.
Box<dyn Trait> moves the implementor into the abstraction, so sharing one implementor across abstractions needs Rc/Arc (plus interior mutability for mutation).

variants.name: Closed-set implementors dispatched by match
variants.idiom_name: enum Renderer plus exhaustive match in the abstraction
variants.implementation_notes: When you own every implementor, model them as an enum and dispatch with match: the abstraction holds the enum by value, so there is no allocation, no vtable and every arm can be inlined, and the compiler checks that no variant is forgotten. This is the same static-versus-dynamic trade the Book describes for trait objects versus generics, taken to its data-oriented extreme - the set is closed, so third-party implementors are impossible without an escape hatch such as wrapping the enum in a dyn trait.
pitfalls: The implementor set is closed: a new variant forces every match over the enum to be updated (which is the point) and recompiles those sites.
Enum alternatives cannot be extended from other crates and all variant data must be known up front, so external implementors require a dyn escape hatch that reintroduces the vtable.
